rules.title: Measure before optimising
rules.what: Never optimise on intuition. Establish a baseline and a functional unit (e.g. one completed search, one rendered page) before changing anything.
rules.why: You only reduce well what you measure. Without a baseline, a change cannot be shown to be an improvement, and effort goes where it feels good instead of where the cost is.
rules.how: Pick the user task that matters, measure its current resource cost (time, bytes, queries, memory), write the numbers down, then optimise the biggest measured cost first.

verify.how: The change ships with before/after numbers on the same functional unit and hardware context.

limits: A measured technical gain is not, by itself, a measured environmental gain.

rules.title: Reduce targets, not just technical metrics
rules.what: Set explicit reduction targets (per functional unit) and review them at regular intervals.
rules.why: A target converts good intentions into a decision rule. Without one, every optimisation competes with every feature for attention, and features always win.
rules.how: Write a target per functional unit (e.g. page weight under 500 KB, API p95 under 200 ms), keep the measurements as evidence, and review at each ecodesign review.

verify.how: A dated document states the target, the measurement method and the last review date.

limits: Targets are project decisions; the rule cannot set their values.

rules.title: Hold regular ecodesign reviews
rules.what: Schedule recurring ecodesign reviews of the service, as you do for security or performance.
rules.why: Sobriety degrades silently: each small addition is reasonable, and the sum is not. Only a recurring review sees the sum.
rules.how: Once per iteration or month, run the audit on the touched areas, review measurements against targets, and record decisions.

verify.how: Review records exist and are dated.

rules.title: Standard, open, interoperable technologies
rules.what: Prefer open formats and standard, interoperable technologies over proprietary lock-in for data and interfaces.
rules.why: Open formats keep data portable and tools replaceable, which extends the useful life of the service and its content beyond one vendor's roadmap.
rules.how: Use JSON/CSV/Markdown over docx/xlsx for data exchange; HTML over proprietary formats for documents; document the exit path for any proprietary dependency.

patterns.note: Binary office formats used as data exchange; legitimate as final documents.

verify.how: List the data formats in use; each closed format has a stated reason.

limits: Interop has a runtime cost of its own; this rule is about lifecycle, not bytes.

rules.title: State the functional unit and the boundary
rules.what: Every resource comparison states what is measured (functional unit), on what boundary (client, network, server, datacentre) and on what hardware.
rules.why: A gain on one boundary can be a transfer to another. Without the stated boundary, numbers from different measurements get compared and wrong conclusions follow.
rules.how: Name the unit ('one search completed'), the boundary (browser CPU, transferred bytes, server CPU), and the hardware or cloud context, before quoting any number.

verify.how: Any reported gain cites unit, boundary, method, sample size.

rules.title: Check the rebound before claiming a win
rules.what: Before claiming a win, check whether the change makes usage grow in a way that cancels the saving.
rules.why: An optimisation that makes a feature cheaper often makes it more used. Efficiency without a usage boundary can increase total consumption.
rules.how: Pair each efficiency claim with the observed usage change over a relevant period; report both.

verify.how: Usage metric before/after accompanies the efficiency metric.

limits: Rebound analysis needs a usage period; not available for new features.
